name: Omar Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the big 400-ton stamping press at Delmar Auto Parts, making door reinforcement panels. I start at six, change the die when the order changes, and that's a four-hour job with the crane and two helpers. In between I watch for cracks and burrs on the panels and keep the press log. After thirty-six years I can tell a bad die by the sound.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You've been there a long time. What keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay is good, the people are my people, and I'm good at it. Honestly, nobody asks me to do anything new these days, and I like it that way. The younger ones use tablets for the checks. I use the clipboard and I'm right about as often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've heard this one before. At work I'd tell the lads to do their jobs and not believe everything. To friends I'd say the news says every year it's the end of everything and then the press still needs a die.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I don't use any of it and I don't feel I'm missing anything. What I do worry about is our biggest customer, who's moving some orders overseas. That's a bigger threat to my shifts than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do. Same press, same hours. I'd keep paying my share into the pension and I'd start thinking seriously about what age I stop, perhaps 61 if the orders keep dropping. Lucia, my wife, keeps asking me for a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it's nothing to do with AI. It's the orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the plant under any other pressure that you already worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. They've dropped about a fifth in two years and the manager says it's temporary. I've heard that word before. I'd say we're fine until we're not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone at work who's excited about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to use it if it helps and leave me out of it. I'm too old to learn a new tablet, and I'm too good with the old way to need to.

say: We've heard this one before; do your job and don't believe everything.
The press still needs a **die**, whatever the news says.
think: I don't use AI and don't feel I'm missing anything.
My real worry is our biggest customer moving **orders** overseas.
do: Carry on with the same press and the same hours.
Keep paying into my **pension** and think about stopping at 61.
Give Lucia a retirement **date** to plan around.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, but it's the orders, not AI.
S0.quote: The news says every year it's the end of everything and then the press still needs a die.
fieldNote: His unease is about **orders** drying up, not AI.
Resists new tools but has a clear head about what matters.
Retirement date talk with his wife is a live theme.

steps.text: Keep running the 400-ton press on the same shift
Pay extra into the pension each month this year
Tell Lucia a retirement date by the spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the front office feels it first. Planning, ordering steel, answering the customers' queries. We have a small team, three people, and I'd expect it to go down to one with some program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I think the floor stays about the same for a while, but the plant gets leaner, and a lean plant is a smaller plant. I can't prove it, but when the office shrinks, the floor usually follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not change much. I'd hand the new tools to the young ones on my shift and let them handle it. I'd put some money into a safe account in case the hours get cut, and I'd ask the manager a straight question about the future of the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more than I let on. I know it's not my work, but it affects the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the plant would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three people in the office, then the quality checkers with the tablets. Rosa in planning is 55 and she won't find it easy to move jobs. I'd feel for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager how many shifts we have by next year. He'll say it's fine, and I'll watch what he does, not what he says.

I'd ask my manager straight about the future of the line.

Move some money into a safe account in case hours get cut.
Ask my manager how many shifts we have by next year.
feel: **Anxious**, more than I let on, because it would affect the whole plant.
S1.quote: When the office shrinks, the floor usually follows.
fieldNote: He reads the plant's **trajectory** from the office outwards.

steps.text: Ask the manager how many shifts the line has next year
Move two months of wages into a safe savings account
Keep running the press and let the young ones use the new tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and no one's ready. At work we'd all be talking about it at lunch and nobody would know. I'd say the government needs to stop the firms cutting before there's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think I've got until around 2031 before the robots arrive at the press. They've had arms on stamping lines for years already, so I've watched that coming. The difference is robots that can change the die and handle the odd jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting money away harder and I'd bring forward my stop date to the earliest I can afford. I'd talk to Lucia about downsizing the house, now the kids are gone. And I'd tell the young ones on my shift to look for work with a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and tired. It would feel like the end of a trade I've been proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for retraining that's real and a decent early pension for people my age. I'd want it so a man who's given forty years can leave with some dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at work in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down at work, because the old way is the only thing I'm sure about. But I'd go and see the pension advisor within the month.

At lunch nobody would know what to say, and I'd say so out loud.
think: I've watched robot arms on stamping lines for years, but robots that change the **die** are the new thing.
I'd have until about 2031 before they reach my press.
do: Bring forward my **stop date** to the earliest I can afford.

See the **pension advisor** within the month.
feel: **Anxious** and tired, like the end of a trade I'm proud of.
S2.quote: I'd want it so a man who's given forty years can leave with some dignity.
fieldNote: His fear is not tech but **dignity** at the end of a long career.

steps.text: Book the pension advisor and ask for the earliest affordable stop date
Put extra money into savings from every pay packet
Talk with Lucia about selling the house and downsizing
Press the union and government for an early pension scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more breathing room, but it's still quick. At work I'd say the older ones should think about their end date now and the younger ones about a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, in this one I'd probably be gone before the robots reach the stamping press in 2034. I'd be 66. My question is whether the plant even survives that long, with orders going overseas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd choose a date, probably 62, and plan towards it. I'd carry on with the press, keep my head down and save. I'd also sit down with the apprentices, Kiran and Josh, and show them everything I know about the die, because that knowledge shouldn't be lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as bad. I feel like I could see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kiran, who's 24 and has a mortgage, and Rosa in planning. I'd tell Kiran to find a trade that's about people, like an electrician who goes to the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything bigger than the robots that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plant is the thing I worry about. If it shuts in 2031, none of this matters to me. I'd be 63 with a pension but I'd lose the friends.

say: Five years is **breathing room**, but still quick; older ones should pick an end date now.
The younger ones should start looking at a **new trade** this year.
think: I'd probably be gone before the robots reach the press in 2034.
My real question is whether the **plant** survives that long.
do: Choose a stop date of **62** and plan towards it.
Show the apprentices, Kiran and Josh, everything I know about the die.
Keep saving and keep my head down.
feel: **Anxious**, but less so, because I can see it coming.
S3.quote: I'd tell Kiran to find a trade that's about people, like an electrician who goes to the house.
fieldNote: He turns his retirement into a **knowledge handover** to the apprentices.
The plant closing matters more to him than robots.
Advice to the young comes from practical trades, not tech.

steps.text: Pick 62 as my stop date and tell the manager
Show Kiran and Josh how to read and set the big die
Keep saving the same amount every month
Keep running the press and logging every run on paper

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different story. I'd say it's enough time for the country to plan, and for people like Kiran to choose a good second trade. I'd tell the firm to start talking to the unions now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be retired for six years by 2036. It's not my problem. I'd care about the town, though. If the plant closes, half the shops on the high street go with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 61 or 62 and then enjoy the allotment and the grandkids. I'd keep a bit saved for the grandkids' studies. And I'd go to a council meeting about the town's future once or twice, because somebody should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly for the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope for the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's still making panels, with people and machines together. I'd rather see old men and robots working side by side than an empty building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's ten years, I'm out and happy. I'd be sorry for the ones who aren't.

say: Ten years is **enough time** for the country to plan and for young people to choose a second trade.
I'd tell the firm to start talking to the **unions** now.
think: I'd be retired for six years by 2036, so it's the **town** I'd care about.
If the plant closes, half the shops on the high street go with it.

Keep some savings aside for the grandkids' studies.
Go to a council meeting about the town's future.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mostly for the town rather than for me.
S4.quote: If the plant closes, half the shops on the high street go with it.
fieldNote: Long horizon turns his concern into the **town** and his grandchildren.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the one where nobody gets the time to adjust and the firms decide it all. What would help is a decent early pension and a plan from the government that says what happens to the towns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, just that I'm not against anything. I'm only saying leave a man his dignity at the end of forty years on the floor.

headlineQuote: I'm only saying leave a man his dignity at the end of forty years on the floor.
portrait: Omar (**58**, runs a 400-ton stamping press at an auto-parts plant) is secure on money and ready for retirement.
He never uses AI tools and keeps to his **clipboard** and his ears, trusting his skill over screens.
His unease comes from a shrinking order book and the fate of the town, more than from AI itself.
As the scenarios speed up, he plans an **early exit** and a handover to the apprentices.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most because firms decide alone and nobody has time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: A decent **early pension** and a government plan for what happens to towns like his.
